planting.note: Plant the dormant tuber 3-4 inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil once the ground has warmed, choosing a site shielded from late cold snaps.

directions: Native to the Khasia Hills of northeastern India, this compact jack-in-the-pulpit forms a slowly offsetting clump of trifoliate green leaves topped by an early-summer flower with an unusual brush-tipped spadix. The common name refers to a pale patch on the reverse of the spathe hood where it curls downward. Grow it in part sun to light shade in soil that stays evenly moist through spring but drains well, and mulch lightly over winter dormancy. Because it slowly multiplies by offsets rather than seed, division of established clumps is the most reliable way to increase stock.

planting.note: Set tubers 4 inches deep in rich, humus-laden woodland soil in a sheltered spot once hard frosts have passed, since this high-elevation species resents being forced too early.

directions: Collected from the Gaoligong Shan range of western Yunnan and first described in 1977, this species was long considered too closely tied to cold high-Himalayan relatives to grow easily, yet it has proven adaptable in ordinary woodland gardens. Large trifoliate leaves rise on a sturdy petiole beneath a hooded, dark purple spathe streaked with yellow veining and drawn out into a long tapering spadix tail. Plant in part sun to light shade with consistent moisture during the growing season, allowing the tuber to go dry and dormant through fall and winter. It pairs well with other Sino-Himalayan arisaemas that share its preference for cool, humus-rich soil.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in loose, moisture-retentive woodland soil in mid-spring, leaving room for the slightly stoloniferous roots to wander and form new offshoots.

directions: Native to Nepal and Tibet, this species takes its botanical name from the absence of the whip-like appendage that extends from the spadix in many other jack-in-the-pulpits. Whorled, umbrella-like foliage unfurls atop upright stems in spring, followed in May by a nearly closed, erect spathe. Because the roots creep gently outward like those of Arisaema concinnum, allow extra space between tubers so offsets have room to establish. Keep the planting site in part sun to light shade with even moisture during active growth and allow it to dry out once the foliage yellows for the summer.

planting.note: Set the dormant rhizome 4-5 inches deep in deep, fertile woodland soil in spring, allowing generous room since this is among the tallest species in the genus.

directions: Described from Ehime Prefecture on the Japanese island of Shikoku, this is a strikingly large jack-in-the-pulpit with horseshoe-shaped leaflets carried atop tall stems, placing it morphologically between the more familiar Arisaema serratum and Arisaema tosaense. A compact green pitcher-shaped spathe sits just above the foliage on a short secondary stalk, enclosing a dark, club-shaped spadix. Site it in light to full shade with rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, and give it room to reach its full stature before crowding it with neighboring perennials. Established clumps slowly produce offset rhizomes that can be divided for propagation.

planting.note: Plant the small tuber 3 inches deep in sharply drained, humus-amended soil in spring; this high-elevation species tolerates drier conditions than most arisaemas but still wants cool roots.

directions: This diminutive species grows wild in dry, open sites between 7,000 and 10,000 feet in the Sichuan and Yunnan provinces of China, and is a close relative of the better-known Arisaema candidissimum and Arisaema fargesii. Trifoliate leaves with a subtle blue-green cast emerge alongside a short flowering stalk bearing a green, purple-striped pulpit and a small curved black spadix hidden beneath the arched hood. It performs best where winters are reliably cold, slowing down or sulking in warmer gardens, so site it in part sun to light shade with gritty, well-drained soil that is not kept constantly wet. Divide offsets after the foliage dies back for summer dormancy.

planting.note: Set the dormant tuber 4 inches deep in deep, fertile, evenly moist woodland soil in spring, giving it room to develop into one of the larger-statured species in the genus.

directions: Native to southern Japan, this robust and seldom-grown species produces two broad leaves, each divided into roughly a dozen leaflets arranged in a horseshoe pattern. A green, jack-in-the-pulpit-style flower is carried on a short stalk just above the foliage canopy in spring. Grow it in light to full shade with rich, humus-laden soil that stays evenly moist during active growth, letting the tuber rest dry once the leaves senesce in late summer. Its substantial size makes it a strong structural anchor among smaller woodland shade perennials.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in spring; this is one of the more forgiving and vigorous cobra lilies for beginners.

directions: Found growing abundantly across parts of Yunnan Province in China, this cobra lily is distinguished from its relatives by long, narrow, three-lobed leaves. In late spring a vividly green-and-white striped pitcher opens to reveal a slender, snake-like green spadix emerging from the mouth of the hood. It is notably easier and more vigorous in cultivation than many Asian arisaemas, tolerating a range of part-sun to shaded woodland conditions as long as soil stays humus-rich and evenly moist through the growing season. Divide offsets from the base of established clumps once plants go dormant in fall.
